trial_name: Low-Dose Dopamine in Early Renal Dysfunction (ANZICS CTG, 2000)
citation: Bellomo R, Chapman M, Finfer S, Hickling K, Myburgh J; Australian and New Zealand Intensive Care Society Clinical Trials Group. Low-dose dopamine in patients with early renal dysfunction: a placebo-controlled randomised trial. Lancet. 2000;356:2139-2143.
one_liner: In ICU patients with SIRS and early renal dysfunction, low-dose dopamine (2 µg/kg/min) did not reduce peak serum creatinine, need for renal replacement therapy, or mortality compared with placebo.

pico.population: Adults in ICU with ≥2 SIRS criteria and early renal dysfunction (oliguria or rising creatinine)
pico.outcome: Peak serum creatinine during infusion (primary); renal replacement therapy, mortality, etc.

background.existing_knowledge: Renal-dose dopamine (1–3 µg/kg/min) was widely used in critical care to increase renal blood flow, augment urine output, and prevent progression from early renal dysfunction to acute renal failure.
background.knowledge_gap: No definitive blinded RCT had tested whether low-dose dopamine improved clinically important renal outcomes in the target population.
background.hypothesis: Low-dose dopamine would reduce biochemical worsening of renal function and improve renal outcomes and mortality.

methods.design: Multicentre, randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 23 ICUs in Australia and New Zealand.
methods.setting: 23 ICUs in Australia and New Zealand; enrolled March 1996 to April 1999.

inclusion: Adults with ≥2 SIRS criteria in prior 24 h

Early renal dysfunction: urine output <0.5 mL/kg/h for ≥4 h, or serum creatinine >150 µmol/L with no premorbid renal dysfunction, or rise in creatinine >80 µmol/L in <24 h without CK >5000 IU/L and without myoglobinaemia
exclusion: Acute renal failure in prior 3 months
Dopamine use at any dose during current ICU stay
Inability to administer trial drug for ≥8 h

methods.intervention: Continuous IV dopamine 2 µg/kg/min via central venous catheter, prepared off-ward, replaced every 24 h.
methods.comparison: Identical placebo infusion with same procedures.
methods.blinding: Double-blind; allocation concealed; study drug indistinguishable.
methods.sample_size_power: Planned 115 per group for 20% reduction in peak creatinine; increased to >300 after interim analyses; final 328 randomised, 324 analysed.
secondary_outcomes: Increase in serum creatinine from baseline
methods.follow_up: To ICU discharge and hospital discharge.

headline_bullets: Peak creatinine nearly identical: 245 vs 249 µmol/L (P=0.93)
No reduction in RRT: 35 vs 40 patients (P=0.55)
No difference in renal recovery or other secondary outcomes

outcomes_table.outcome: Increase in serum creatinine from baseline (µmol/L)

outcomes_table.note: Study drug stopped for suspected arrhythmia in 7 vs 7 patients

outcomes_table.outcome: Time to renal recovery after stopping infusion

safety: Cardiac arrhythmias: 53 vs 54 patients; study drug stopped for suspected arrhythmia in 7 vs 7 patients.

domains.notes: Allocation sequence held by independent pharmacist/nurse; drug preparation off-ward with identical infusions; concealment robust.
Double-blind; primary and secondary outcomes were objective laboratory values and hard clinical endpoints, reducing detection bias.
4 patients excluded post-randomisation (2 per group), yielding 161 vs 163 analysed; symmetric attrition reduces but does not eliminate risk of bias.
Mean infusion duration similar (113 vs 125 h, P=0.45); study drug discontinuation for arrhythmia identical (7 vs 7); dopamine use during ICU stay was an exclusion criterion, minimising crossover.
Groups well matched: APACHE II 18 vs 18, shock 93 vs 102, ventilation 138 vs 141, baseline creatinine 183 vs 182 µmol/L.

Powered for surrogate primary endpoint; confidence intervals for renal markers narrow and centred near zero, supporting no clinically relevant effect; underpowered for mortality and modest RRT differences.

internal_validity.verdict: Strong for primary biochemical endpoint; moderate for clinical endpoints due to limited power.

domains.notes: High-acuity ICU patients with SIRS and early renal dysfunction (many ventilated, in shock) reflect the population where renal-dose dopamine was used. Excluded advanced AKI (creatinine >300 µmol/L), recent ARF, transplant, and patients unsuitable for RRT.
23 ICUs in Australia and New Zealand; generalisable to similar high-resource ICUs with RRT access. Less applicable to resource-limited settings or contemporary vasopressor practices.

external_validity.verdict: Broadly generalisable to adult ICU patients with SIRS and early renal dysfunction in high-resource settings, less applicable to advanced AKI or transplant populations.

strengths: High-risk population with high event rates
Objective primary endpoint with narrow confidence limits
limitations: Primary endpoint was a surrogate marker
Limited power for mortality and modest RRT differences

critical_appraisal.summary: Well-conducted RCT with strong internal validity for biochemical endpoint, but limited power for clinical outcomes; no signal of benefit, supporting abandonment of renal-dose dopamine.

sections.authors_conclusion: Low-dose dopamine did not reduce peak creatinine, progression to severe creatinine thresholds, or need for RRT. Supports abandoning routine renal-dose dopamine as a renoprotective strategy.

clinical_bottom_line.verdict: Does not change practice because it confirms lack of benefit; reinforces existing recommendations against use.
clinical_bottom_line.applies_to: ICU patients with SIRS and early renal dysfunction (oliguria or rising creatinine) who are candidates for RRT.
clinical_bottom_line.does_not_mean: Does not mean dopamine is harmful in all contexts, but no renal benefit was found.
implementation_caveats: Not applicable to advanced AKI (creatinine >300 µmol/L) or transplant patients
Contemporary vasopressor practices may differ, but the negative result is consistent across settings

controversies.notes: The accompanying Lancet editorial emphasised that the physiological narrative persisted despite accumulating negative data, and highlighted plausible off-target harms (endocrine, immune, regional perfusion).
A later meta-analysis concluded that low-dose dopamine may increase urine output but does not prevent renal dysfunction, RRT, or death.
KDIGO recommends against low-dose dopamine for prevention or treatment of AKI.
SSC prioritises norepinephrine and de-emphasises dopamine; renal-dose dopamine not supported as renoprotective adjunct.
Subsequent trials in acute heart failure with renal dysfunction also failed to show renal benefit, suggesting the negative signal is not confined to ICU SIRS cohorts.

unresolved_questions: Whether dopamine-induced diuresis ever translates to renal protection in specific subgroups remains unresolved
Potential off-target harms of low-dose dopamine need further study

quick_recall.one_line_takeaway: Low-dose dopamine does not improve renal function or outcomes in ICU patients with early renal dysfunction; it should not be used for renal protection.
